newsitem.title: USA: US corporate bonds follow Treasuries, issuers busy.
newsitem.headline: US corporate bonds follow Treasuries, issuers busy.

text.p: Prices on investment grade and junk bonds generally tracked Treasuries on Thursday, while most action centered on the primary market, traders said.

U.S. Treasuries rallied at the end of Thursday, recovering from sharp losses prior to the afternoon auction of 30-year bonds. The rally pushed the price on the benchmark 30-year Treasury up more than point, driving yields to 6.53 percent for an eight-month low.
In the primary market, Stuart Entertainment Inc issued $100 million 12.5 percent senior subordinate notes due 2004, rated B3/B-minus, through BT Securities.
Blue Chip Casino Inc sold $85 million of 13 3/4 percent senior secured notes due 2003, rated B3/B-minus, via Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.

Sources say pricing for both deals, which were issued by gaming-related companies, came at the wide range of price talk. Investors have registered concern about the state of the casino industry in the U.S. and demanded higher yield to buy the bonds, they add.
YPF SA, an Argetine oil and gas company, pulled its $200 million debt deal through Merrill Lynch & Co Inc as a result of unfavorable market conditions, sources say.
On a brighter note, Amtrol Inc, an industrial company, increased the size of its senior subordinate note offering to $115 million from $100 million due to strong investor demand.
The notes were rated B3/B-minus and offered a 10 5/8 percent yield. Morgan Stanley was the lead underwriter.
Several investment grade issuers also hit the market on Thursday. They include:
--Korea Development Bank completed a global offering of $500 million seven-year 6 5/8 percent debt through J.P. Morgan Securities Inc and Merrill Lynch.
--Times Mirror Co issued $148 million in 7.25 percent 100-year bonds, rated A1/A-plus, through Merrill.
--Andarko Petroleum sold $100 million in 7.25 percent 100-year debentures, rated A3/BBB-plus, through CS First Boston Corp.
In the secondary market, the cable sector saw considerable activity.
The high-yield debt of Cablevision Systems dropped two to three points, following the company's stock which lost around 20 percent of its market value by the end of Thursday's trading.
Traders said investors reacted negatively to a Wednesday conference call in which officials indicated the company's costs may be on the rise, threatening future profits.
Meanwhile, spreads on Tele-Commmunications Inc paper tightened by five basis points, continuing their recent comeback.
Traders said investor sentiment was buoyed by recent press reports that suggest that competition for cable companies from direct broadcasting system providers may have reached its peak.
